articles.title: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting
articles.summary: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation. It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings.
body: After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.

But what makes a good adaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreau; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equalled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.
points: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true.
But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation.

articles.title: ‘Safe Exit’ Director Mohammed Hammad on Staying True to His Vision: ‘I Need to Be Free as a Filmmaker’
articles.summary: Mohammed Hammad’s “Safe Exit” received an Atlas Prize for Post-production at the 2025 Atlas Workshops of the Marrakech Film Festival before making its debut in the Panorama section of the 2026 Berlinale.
body: How have you negotiated the difficulties of getting an independent film made in Egypt now? “Safe Exit” is completely self-funded. We formed a new production company, Pariedolia Productions, and now we’re trying to distribute the film through that company, which is a challenge. We’ve chosen this model because many studios in Egypt tend to avoid this kind of film, especially given the topics it covers. Even getting the necessary permissions to shoot the film was very hard. But together with my producer Kholoud Saad I knew I needed to make this film, just like we made “Withered Green.”

What about your co-producers? The main co-producer is Dora Bouchoucha with Nomadis Images, from Tunisia. And Ibrahim El-Battout, one of the godfathers of independent cinema in Egypt, is also a co-producer. Ibrahim was with me from the beginning, also as an adviser, and I trust him completely. We worked on pre-production together, in conjunction with Kholoud; Ibrahim is one of Egypt’s leading independent filmmakers, along with Khairy Beshara and Yousry Nasrallah, and he was with us throughout the shooting, every day.

articles.title: Box Office: ‘Street Fighter’ Makes $4 Million in Previews, ‘You Can See Everything’ Behind With $1.75 Million
articles.summary: Several new challengers are stepping into the box office ring this weekend to face off. Paramount’s “Street Fighter” video game adaptation should lead the pack of newcomers. It made $4 million in Thursday previews at the box office, and it’s expected to make $25 million to $35 million in its debut.
body: The highly anticipated Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ” from A24 made $1.75 million in previews and is aiming for third place with $7 million to $8 million, a stellar debut for a non-fiction doc. The movie cost just $7 million to produce and has been building hype since it had a surprise debut at last month’s Telluride Film Festival. Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim secretly filmed Elizabeth Holmes ahead of her 11-year prison sentence and even lived with the disgraced Theranos founder to get full access to her life. It’s expected to be a rare box office hit for a documentary and could even land in this year’s Oscar race.

The final newcomer this weekend is Focus Features’ Jane Austen adaptation of “ Sense and Sensibility,” which cost $25 million and is on track to make $5 million to $8 million this weekend. It made $1.15 million from advance screenings and previews. The new take on the classic novel stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who navigate love, loss and financial uncertainty as they are forced to leave their family estate in Sussex.
points: Paramount’s “Street Fighter” video game adaptation should lead the pack of newcomers.
It made $4 million in Thursday previews at the box office, and it’s expected to make $25 million to $35 million in its debut.

articles.title: Julia Stiles Is ‘Crying’ at ‘DWTS’ Rehearsals Ahead of Heath Ledger Tribute: ‘Bringing Back So Many Memories’
articles.summary: Julia Stiles’ tribute to her “10 Things I Hate About You” co-star Heath Ledger on “Dancing With the Stars” next week is sure to be a teary-eyed performance. “I was crying in rehearsals today,” Stiles told me Thursday at the InStyle Imagemaker Awards in Los Angeles.
body: “One of the things that I’m taking away from this dedication is one of the things that we really hope to do as performers is to make people feel something and have people care about the work that you do, and his memory lives on because it was such an incredible performance,” Stiles said.
Stiles also said that “DWTS” producers had asked her to compete on the show for the past couple of years before she finally agreed to do it.

“I think it was turning 45,” she explained. “I was like, ‘I’m halfway to 90! Why not? It’s now or never.’ I knew that there were going to be emotional hurdles that I’m going to have to get over on this show, like getting over my own nerves, finding my love of performing again, being able to dance in front of an audience, all these things.”

articles.title: Dogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and Romania
articles.summary: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government. As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies.
body: When Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord was shown in Romania as a one-day preview this June, the reception was extraordinary. Across 53 towns and 96 cinemas, the film reportedly pulled in over 40,000 viewers in a single night, a number arthouse cinema rarely sees in Romania. But the response here had little to do with cinema. It felt instead like a reopening of a familiar fault line about the clash of values within the EU itself.

The film echoes events from 2015, when the five children of Marius and Ruth Bodnariu, a Pentecostal couple from Romania living in Norway – part of a Neo-Protestant minority long viewed with suspicion in Orthodox Romania – were removed from their home by Barnevernet, Norway’s child welfare authority, amid concerns over possible corporal punishment and religious indoctrination.

The fallout in Romania stretched on for months, with diplomatic friction, public demonstrations and constant media coverage. The children were eventually returned, and the Bodnarius later resettled in Romania. Mungiu doesn’t retell the story beat for beat, but Romanian viewers had no trouble recognising where it came from.
points: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government.
As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies.

articles.title: Jonathan Glazer says Israel’s retaliation over NAZA ‘more venal’ than anticipated
articles.summary: Film’s executive producer says he was ‘shocked into silence’ the first time he watched documentary that details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The director Jonathan Glazer has called Israel’s retaliation against NAZA’s film-makers and the military figures interviewed in the…
body: Since the film’s release, the Israeli government has denounced it and pursued those involved, announcing plans aimed at stripping citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers; accused NAZA’s co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, of treason; and ordered top legal and security officials to find and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the documentary for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

Speaking to the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.

He noted that it was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.
“Both films deal with dehumanisation,” Glazer said. “And how we get to where we do as a species by othering and dehumanising, and what that then leads to.”

articles.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
articles.summary: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault, all of which he denies.
body: A woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feeling "bewildered and confused".
The woman, who worked at MTV at the time, said the entertainer went from "jovial" to a "wild-eyed maniac" as he attempted, she alleged, to pull her into a toilet.
Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

articles.title: The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable review – Netflix doc on ‘secret album’ is strictly for super fans
articles.summary: The lore of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, once bought by Martin Shkreli, is explored in a rambling film produced by RZA. For every reason except one, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, the seventh album by the Wu-Tang Clan, should’ve been a commercial hit.
body: Azzougarh, who narrates much of the film built around his personal archive (the Disciple doubles as an evolution of digital self-recording, from camcorders to selfies), can be a compelling lead: an unnervingly even-keeled presence, at once well-connected and under-the-radar, who came to the Clan via unrelenting ambition, having connected to their music with fellow immigrant friends, as outsiders in largely white Holland. But centering the bulk of a 105-minute film around one somewhat reticent lead can also prove repetitive and dead-ending, extraneous digressions on the Clan’s Hong Kong film references or tours around Staten Island notwithstanding.

articles.title: Veronica Roth Revives ‘Divergent’ in ‘The Sixth Faction’ (and Talks the Movie That Never Happened)
articles.summary: The author talks carrying “anxiety baggage” about the book series, revisiting the story in an alternate-universe retelling and reflects on the film adaptations never getting an ending: "Everyone had moved forward."
body: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

The Sixth Faction, released on Oct. 6, reimagines Roth’s bestselling series ( Divergent, Insurgent and Allegiant ), which is set in a post-apocalyptic society where citizens are divided into factions based on personality type. The first book in a planned duology is an alternate-universe retelling rather than a prequel or sequel, and it began as a personal project for Roth.

“ Divergent has this staying power that I wasn’t expecting,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s hard for books to have that kind of lingering effect on a readership, and because it had that power, I thought I needed to course-correct my own feelings about it. I’d carried some anxiety baggage about Divergent, and I thought making something new would help me rediscover my love for the characters and the world. That’s where The Sixth Faction came from.”

articles.title: Role Model’s Next Move? He’ll Figure It Out Onstage
articles.summary: The 29-year-old singer, who is currently on his global tour after releasing his third album 'Chuck Timely & the Hourglass,' is embracing his new era with "sunglasses and this weird pathetic drunk guy character."
body: Having his name in lights, being front and center on the stage or on screen was never part of Role Model ‘s plan. Mostly because, “I don’t like anything planned in a show,” he admits.

That might seem a bit stressful for someone who’s juggling a new album, a global tour and his upcoming acting debut in Lena Dunham ‘s Good Sex. But the 29-year-old artist, whose real name is Tucker Harrington Pillsbury, works better just rolling with the punches.

It seems Role Model’s always been this way, even going back to his college days. While he initially went to Point Park University in Pittsburgh to study film, he didn’t anticipate what would happen next.

“While I was in film school, I stumbled across kids that were recording themselves, which I had never seen — just having a mic and Logic in their dorm rooms,” he recalls. “They were like, ‘You should just write a song and just try it.’ And I did and I fell in love with it.”
